'''Fermat’s theorem''' in calculus (also called the '''interior extremum theorem''') states:

If function $f:\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$

* is continuous on $[a,b]$
* and differentiable on $(a,b)$,

$$
\forall c\in(a,b), \\
c \text{ is a local extremum} \Rightarrow \dot{f}(c)=0
$$

<blockquote>
extremum=maximum or minimum
</blockquote>

<blockquote>
'''Warning:''' The reverse of Fermat's theorem, $\dot{f}(c)=0 \Rightarrow c \text{ is a local extremum}$ is '''false'''.

Consider the function $f(x)=x^3$.

$\dot{f}(0)=0$, but $x=0$ is not a local extremum.
</blockquote>

== Proof ==

Suppose $f(x)$ has a local maximum at $x=c$,

$$
\exists \delta \in \mathbb{R}, \delta>0: \forall h \in [-\delta,\delta],\\
f(c+h) \le f(c) \iff f(c+h)-f(c) \le 0,\\
\therefore 
\begin{cases}
\dot{f}(c)=\lim_{h\to 0^+}\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}\le 0, \\
\dot{f}(c)=\lim_{h\to 0^-}\frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h}\ge 0.
\end{cases}
$$

The only way to satisfy both $\dot{f}(c)\le 0$ and $\dot{f}(c) \ge 0$ is:

$$
\dot{f}(c)=0
$$

It can be similarly proven that if $f(x)$ has a local minimum at $x=c$, then $\dot{f}(c)=0$.
